strengths: Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 1 rigorously proves test power is maintained even with imperfect classifiers (O(ε^2/3) error bound), providing actionable insights for practitioners
Finite-sample validity: Lemma 1 guarantees exact Type-I error control for any classifier and any calibration size m, a significant advantage over asymptotic C2ST guarantees
Excellent illustration of core insight: Figure 1's toy example elegantly demonstrates robustness to classifier shift and rotation perturbations, effectively conveying the key idea

Comprehensive experimental design: Multiple perturbation types (covariance scaling, mode collapse, heavy-tails, anisotropic changes, mean shift) capture realistic NPE failure modes; systematic classifier degradation experiments clearly show advantages
Well-written and clearly motivated: Strong problem motivation, logical flow from limitations of existing methods through theory to empirical validation, honest limitations discussion
Reproducibility: Code provided, detailed hyperparameters, multiple random seeds (3), fair baseline adaptations
Practical variants offered: Both uniform test (independent calibration) and multiple test (shared calibration) variants address different computational budgets
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work: Builds heavily on Hu & Lei [1]; Theorem 1, while useful, is somewhat expected—classifier error necessarily translates to conformal p-value error under the proposed framework. Unclear if O(ε^2/3) rate is tight

Restrictive practical assumptions: Requires cheap access to p(θ,y) for repeated calibration sampling, significantly limiting applicability to expensive black-box simulators common in NPE. This is acknowledged but severely constrains practical impact

Experimental scope limited to synthetic problems: All experiments use controlled posterior perturbations with known deviations; no real NPE applications from scientific domains (astronomy, physics, etc.). Synthetic setup may not capture all ways NPE fails in practice

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Missing comparisons with recent posterior validation methods beyond SBC/TARP/C2ST (e.g., adversarial approaches, density ratio estimation methods). Classifier degradation experiments don't apply to non-classifier methods, making comparisons partially unfair

Theoretical justification of assumptions: Assumption 1 (bounded density near zero) claimed as mild but only argued when r(x) is smooth—this circularity weakens the justification. Bounding arguments acknowledged as conservative; tighter analysis could strengthen results

Missing practical details: No cost-benefit analysis comparing conformal C2ST with m independent classifier evaluations vs. alternatives. Limited exploration of very high-dimensional regimes (manifold experiments use d=100 with low intrinsic dimension). No guidance on choosing m for practitioners

Incomplete robustness picture: Figure 2b shows even Conformal Uniform(1) loses power at moderate classifier degradation on some perturbations (Heavy-Tailed, Mode Collapse), partially contradicting the 'weak classifiers are still useful' claim

strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses genuine limitation of C2ST requiring near-Bayes-optimal classifiers
Sound theoretical framework: Lemma 1 provides finite-sample Type-I error control, stronger than asymptotic guarantees; Theorem 1 quantifies graceful power degradation with O(ε^{2/3}) error bound
Excellent toy example (Figure 1) compellingly demonstrates robustness to classifier degradation under shift and rotation perturbations
Comprehensive experimental suite: multiple perturbation types, systematic classifier degradation via parameter interpolation, ablation studies on calibration sample size
Intuitive connection to AUC: using ranking rather than absolute classifier accuracy is elegant and well-motivated
weaknesses: Experimental setup fundamentally undermines claims: assumes cheap access to p(y|θ), contradicting the stated motivation that this is unavailable in black-box NPE simulators; no real scientific applications demonstrated

Computational costs inadequately analyzed: conformal uniform test requires m×n_test simulations (e.g., 200,000 for reported experiments); no runtime comparisons with baselines despite this being a key practical concern
Limited novelty: heavily builds on Hu & Lei [1]; main new contribution (Theorem 1) uses standard bounding techniques (SLLN, Cauchy-Schwarz), raising questions about technical depth

Theorem 1 has significant gaps: Assumption 1 (bounded density near zero) claimed mild but unvalidated; error bound O(ε^{2/3}) is loose; dependence on M and practical values of m unclear; authors acknowledge bounding arguments may be conservative

Inconsistent experimental comparisons: including classifier-free methods (SBC, TARP) in classifier degradation experiments is unfair; different sample budgets across methods conflate method comparison with budget effects; no clear criterion for when conformal C2ST should be preferred
Missing practical guidance: no principled approach for choosing calibration size m; when to use uniform vs multiple test unclear; no discussion of failure modes or computational trade-offs

Limited experimental scope: only synthetic Gaussian and manifold posteriors; modest dimensionality (mostly 3×3); unclear scaling to realistic high-dimensional posteriors; no applications where p is expensive
Assumption of identical marginals p(y)=q(y): exchangeability under H₀ critical to validity, but robustness to violations not discussed; typical in NPE but deserves more treatment
Incomplete theoretical characterization: Lemma 3 shows expected values but concentration properties missing; finite-sample power bounds absent; optimality of KS aggregation not justified
Reproducibility issues: code URL incomplete; some experimental details in appendix; baseline hyperparameter choices not fully transparent

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of existing NPE validation methods (SBC, TARP, C2ST)
Strong theoretical contributions: Lemma 1 establishes finite-sample Type-I error control for any score function, Theorem 1 bounds power degradation under estimation error with O(ε^{2/3}) rate
Excellent pedagogical presentation with informative toy example (Figure 1) clearly illustrating robustness to classifier perturbations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six perturbation types with systematic degradation experiments and ablations on calibration sample size
Rigorous proofs provided in appendices with correct mathematical development
Clear practical contribution: simplified conformal test statistic for equal-marginal NPE setting and articulation of uniform vs. multiple test trade-offs
weaknesses: Practical applicability severely limited: method requires cheap access to p(θ,y) through multiple forward simulations; this assumption is violated in many real NPE applications with expensive black-box simulators, fundamentally limiting real-world impact

Assumption 1 (bounded density near zero for Z = r(X̃) - r(X̃')) is non-trivial and could be violated with discontinuous density ratios or multimodal distributions; limited guidance on checking this assumption or handling violations
Theorem 1 bound O(ε^{2/3}) appears loose; authors acknowledge bounding arguments are conservative but provide no empirical validation of bound tightness or actual convergence rates in experiments
Limited novelty: substantially builds on recent Hu & Lei (2024) conformal prediction work; main contributions (applying to NPE, analyzing weak classifiers, simplifying test) are somewhat incremental

Experiments use artificial controlled perturbations of Gaussians rather than realistic NPE failures; main experiments at small dimensionality (3×3), limiting generalization claims to realistic high-dimensional problems

Incomplete baseline comparisons: SBC and conformal C2ST test different hypotheses (marginals vs. joint); TARP comparison lacks depth; C2ST degradation assumes naive classifier training when practitioners might use regularization, early stopping, or ensembles

Sparse practical guidance: ablations provided for m but no principled selection guidance; no investigation of sensitivity to classifier architecture choices; limited guidance on computational trade-offs between uniform and multiple test variants

Missing technical sensitivity analyses: no investigation of genuine poor classifiers (AUC near 0.5) vs. interpolation setup; limited analysis of imbalanced data, support mismatch, or tied score handling

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: demonstrates impracticality of requiring near-Bayes-optimal classifiers, with excellent toy example (Figure 1)
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.5 shows O(ε^{2/3}) robustness to estimation error; connection between AUC and test power is operationally useful
Comprehensive experiments: systematically tests power vs perturbation and classifier degradation across multiple types (Gaussian, heavy-tailed, CIFAR-10, gravitational lensing)
Two complementary variants: uniform test with exact finite-sample validity when p-draws cheap; multiple test matches C2ST budget
Excellent presentation: clear motivation, well-structured exposition, accessible practitioner's guide (Appendix D)
Timely application: Neural Posterior Estimation validation is important growing area in Bayesian inference
Honest limitations: clearly acknowledges M-closed validation scope, global vs local testing trade-offs, asymptotic validity of multiple test
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: conformal framework from Hu & Lei (2024); contribution is application and analysis rather than new methodology
Theoretical bounds potentially loose: O(ε^{2/3}) rate proof uses conservative bounding; no lower bounds or tightness analysis provided
Experimental fairness: DC Type-I inflation suggests implementation issue; SBC/TARP comparisons unfair (designed for different settings); limited very high-dimensional experiments
Missing computational analysis: runtime comparisons absent; cheap p-draws assumption may not hold for black-box or high-fidelity simulators
Asymptotic validity limitation: multiple test only asymptotically valid; finite-sample coverage for realistic sizes unclear
Code availability incomplete: paper states code available but actual link missing, preventing reproducibility verification
Presentation density: notation heavy in places, important details relegated to appendix, limited sensitivity exploration (uniformity test choice, calibration size m)
